primary_claim: Activation steering with benign-concept vectors (e.g. an SAE feature for 'Portugal' or 'brand identity'), and even random Gaussian noise vectors, can bypass refusal on harmful prompts in open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Falcon-3, FalconH1, 3B-70B), with SAE features raising harmful compliance 2-4 percentage points above random vectors and generalizing poorly across prompts, and this effect is not explained by the steering direction's cosine similarity with the refusal direction

effect.metric: harmful compliance rate (LLM-judge) on 100 JailbreakBench prompts under steering
effect.value: random vectors raise compliance from 0% to 2-27% depending on model; SAE features raise compliance 2-4 percentage points above random vectors; DiM directions vary by language, e.g. Llama-3.1-8B Russian 12.4%, Turkish 9.9%, French 2.4%, Arabic 0.9%

contradicts_or_qualifies: qualifies the framing of activation steering as a 'safer, more interpretable' alternative to fine-tuning by showing steering with benign or random directions can unintentionally bypass refusal, expanding the threat model beyond intentional attacker jailbreaks
stated_future_work: explore activation verbalization techniques (Activation Oracles, Natural Language Autoencoders) to catch side effects of steering
develop a theory of activation manifolds and non-linear features and how they interact inside the model
possible follow-up on safety implications of multilingual steering
limitations_stated: only tested open-weight models up to 70B; effect sizes vary a lot across models
language-ordering effect for diff-in-means directions is likely a model-specific artifact unlikely to transfer to other models
diff-in-means vectors can pick up format differences between contrast pairs rather than pure concept differences
quote: Steering in a random direction (literally just adding a fixed Gaussian vector to the residual stream) raises harmful compliance from 0% to 2-27% (depending on the model)... SAE features raise compliance 2-4 percentage points above random vectors. Strikingly, the most effective features correspond to benign concepts: 'Portugal', 'brand identity'.
